(1) humans and machines can rank and classify speech recognition hypotheses, (2) humans are better than machines at ranking but machines are better than humans at classification, (3) humans and machines benefit from the dialogue context when ranking and classifying speech recognition hypotheses and (4) machines can outperform humans at re-ranking speech recognition hypotheses.

(i) human subjects can be used to collect training data for machine learning classifiers, (ii) machine learning classifiers can outperform human subjects, and (iii) machine learning classifiers are more consistent than human subjects.

The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to improve the performance of a dialogue system by using contextual information available at run-time.
it is feasible to re-rank and classify N-Best hypotheses automatically and that it is possible to improve recognition results by using the information from the dialogue context.
the dialogue context, which can be used to re-rank and classify recognition hypotheses, is an important factor for improving recognition accuracy and for grounding recognition results.
